chapters.title: About Rudyard Kipling and His Stories

pages.text: Rudyard Kipling was born in Bombay, India, in 1865, and grew up between India and England. He won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1907. He wrote novels, poetry, and short stories. Among the most beloved of his works are his Just So Stories, published in 1902, originally told to his daughter Josephine.

image.note: Illustration: a father reading aloud to a child by firelight, a jungle scene visible through the window

pages.text: The Just So Stories are origin stories, comic and playful explanations of how animals came to be the way they are. How the Whale got his throat. How the Camel got his hump. How the Leopard got his spots. How the Elephant got his trunk. They are told in a distinctive voice, warm, ceremonial, and slightly pompous in a way that is clearly affectionate. The repeated phrase Just So, an instruction from a child to a parent, is embedded in the stories' DNA: this is exactly how it happened, and do not change a word.

Kipling's work carries the attitudes of his era and requires a reader's awareness of its historical context. The stories presented here are selected for their storytelling virtues. They are told by someone who loved animals, language, and the pleasure of an explanation that is completely satisfying even when utterly invented.

chapters.title: How the Elephant Got His Trunk (Extended)

pages.text: Once, a very long time ago, the elephant had no trunk. He had only a blackish, bulgy nose, as big as a boot, that he could wriggle about from side to side, but could not pick things up with.

image.note: Illustration: an elephant with a tiny boot-sized nose, looking puzzled at a piece of fruit on the ground

pages.text: The elephant's child was full of satiable curiosity: he wanted to know everything about everything, and most particularly what the Crocodile had for dinner. All his relatives spanked him for asking too many questions. He asked the Kolokolo Bird, who told him to go to the great grey-green greasy Limpopo River to find out. At the river, the Crocodile offered to whisper the answer if the elephant's child came closer. The Crocodile grabbed his nose and pulled.

The elephant's child pulled back with all his strength. He pulled and the Crocodile pulled, and as they pulled, the elephant's child's nose stretched and stretched. Eventually the Crocodile let go and the elephant's child sat down hard on the bank with a nose that now reached nearly to the ground.

At first he was displeased. But then he discovered that the stretched nose could pick up grass, could carry bundles, could spray water, could wave away flies, and could deliver a satisfying smack to the relatives who had spanked him. After some weeks, all the other elephants went to the Limpopo River and asked the Crocodile to stretch their noses too.

Kipling wrote these tales for his own children, and he was fierce about how they must be told: not one word changed, the same funny voice every time, or the child would object. That is where the name comes from. If you have ever demanded a bedtime story be told exactly, exactly as it was last night, you already understand the Just So Stories. They are less about how the animals really got their shapes than about the pleasure of a story told the same delicious way again and again.

chapters.title: How the Camel Got His Hump

pages.text: In the beginning, when the world was new and the animals were just beginning to work for the man, the Camel refused to do anything at all. He lived in the middle of a Howling Desert and ate thorns and tamarisks and prickles and milkweed, and said 'Humph!' to anyone who asked him to help.

image.note: Illustration: a camel standing apart from working horses, oxen, and dogs, looking disdainful

pages.text: The horse, the ox, and the dog complained to the Djinn of All Deserts. The Djinn went to the Camel. 'You have not worked at all,' said the Djinn, 'and so you are to be humped.' He worked a Djinn-magic over the Camel, and the Camel's back rose and puffed up into a great big hump. 'That is your very own hump,' said the Djinn, 'and you have made it yourself through being so idle. But now you can go and work, for you can live on your hump for three days without eating or drinking, and make up for all the days that you missed.'
And the Camel has had a hump ever since.

chapters.title: How the Leopard Got His Spots

pages.text:
The next story uses characters and language that reflect Kipling's era and its attitudes. Read it as a product of its time, and notice the pleasure Kipling takes in the sheer absurdity of his explanation.

In the beginning, the Leopard lived on a sandy-yellow plain and was sandy-yellow all over. He hunted alongside a man called the Ethiopian, who was also sandy-yellow. Together they hunted giraffe and zebra and quagga. But then the giraffe and zebra and quagga moved into the forest, where the broken light and shadow made their spots and stripes the best possible camouflage.

image.note: Illustration: a spotted giraffe perfectly camouflaged against dappled forest light; a confused sandy-yellow leopard looking for it

pages.text: The Ethiopian turned himself dark brown to blend into the shadow, and was very pleased with the result. He then painted the Leopard all over with his fingers, making spots of dark against the sandy ground colour, and the Leopard was delighted. Then they both went into the forest, and they did very well indeed.

'But why didn't you paint your own spots first?' the Leopard asked the Ethiopian. 'Spots are good,' said the Ethiopian, 'but given the choice between spots and being able to change your spots at will, I prefer the flexibility.' And that is how the Ethiopian came to be the colour he is, and why the Leopard has his spots, and it is perfectly and completely just so.

There is a tale of how the first letter was written, and how the alphabet came after. A little girl called Taffy, long ago before anyone could write, tries to send a picture message to fetch her father's spear, and the picture is so badly misunderstood that it causes chaos in the whole tribe. But from that muddle grows an idea: that pictures could stand for sounds, and sounds could be joined, and marks on bark could carry a message across distance with no mistake. Writing, Kipling suggests, was invented by a child.

It is a playful notion, and like all the Just So Stories it is not meant to be believed, only enjoyed. Yet underneath the nonsense sits something true: writing really was one of humanity's greatest inventions, and it really did change everything. Kipling dresses the truth in a funny story about a little girl and a misunderstood picture, and the truth goes down all the more easily for the laughter. That is the trick these tales perform, over and over.

chapters.title: The Crab That Played with the Sea

pages.text: Before the world was quite finished, the Eldest Magician called all the animals and gave each of them their character and their way of living. The Crab, however, was not where he was supposed to be. He was in the sea, playing.

image.note: Illustration: an enormous crab in a vast dark sea, completely unbothered, while the other animals line up on shore

pages.text: The Eldest Magician was displeased. But the Crab, who had been playing in the sea since before the world was finished, made his case simply: 'This is where I was when you called. This is what I was doing. I was not told to stop.' The Eldest Magician considered this. He could find no flaw in the Crab's logic. The Crab had been doing exactly what crabs do. 'Very well,' said the Eldest Magician. 'Carry on.' And the Crab does. It is the only animal that was given permission directly to do exactly what it was already doing.
And that is why the Crab walks sideways and will not be hurried, even now.
